attempts_log.asr_text: On September 3rd, 2026, a medical journal published a new gene treatment for hard-to-treat autoimmune diseases of the nervous system. The study included 16 people, seven with progressive multiple sclerosis and three each with MOG antibody-associated disease, generalized myasthenia gravis, and idiopathic inflammatory muscle disease. The unusual part was where the treatment was made. Instead of removing a patient's immune cells, changing them in a laboratory, and putting them back, researchers gave one intravenous dose of a disabled gene carrier. It delivered a gene for CD19-targeting CAR T cells into the patient's own T cells inside the body.

full_story_part1.canonical_text:
On September 3, 2026, a medical journal published a report on a new gene treatment for hard-to-treat autoimmune diseases of the nervous system.

The study included 16 people: seven with progressive multiple sclerosis, and three each with MOG-antibody-associated disease, generalized myasthenia gravis, and idiopathic inflammatory muscle disease.

The unusual part was where the treatment was made.

Instead of removing a patient’s immune cells, changing them in a laboratory, and putting them back, researchers gave one intravenous dose of a disabled gene carrier. It delivered a gene for CD19-targeting CAR-T cells into the patient’s own T cells inside the body.

full_story_part2.text: In other words, the body itself became the place where the CAR-T cells were produced. After treatment, deep changes in B cells were reported. The study also described improvements in neurological function, symptoms, antibody levels, and muscle-related blood tests across the 4 disease groups. The safety findings were also closely watched. 11 of the 16 participants developed a mild, grade 1 immune reaction called cytokine release syndrome during the first 4 weeks. The symptoms, including short-term fever, eased within 2 weeks in all 11 people. The study did not report immune-related nerve toxicity, low blood pressure, or low oxygen.

point_one.text: The most important shared signal was not that every patient improved in the same way. B cells fell deeply in the blood, bone marrow, and spinal fluid, then began to return at a median of about 2 months. This gives researchers a measurable, temporary immune change to track while the clinical signals differ from one disease to another.

point_two.text: The report cannot show that the treatment caused the improvements. There were only 16 participants, no comparison group, and some disease groups had 3 people while one had 7. A larger controlled study must follow patients as B cells return and test whether the changes last and exceed other possible explanations, including normal disease fluctuation.

in_one_line.text: This study offers an early glimpse of a one-dose treatment that builds CD19 CAR-T cells inside the body and deeply reduces B-cell levels, with B cells beginning to re-emerge at a median of about 2 months in participants with several difficult diseases. The signal is promising, but a lasting treatment effect still needs to be proven.
